items.title: Hollywood Is Squeezing Producers to Death (and Killing the Industry in the Process)
items.summary: I got up yesterday morning and did something I hate. I drove to one of my favorite coffee shops in Los Angeles and had a goodbye coffee and bagel with a producer I've known for 15 years. They were leaving the industry not because their passion had waned, but because the town no longer supports most producers financially. This particular producer has made films and TV shows that millions of you have watched, but since COVID, they have found it increasingly hard to get paid. That's because Hollywood is squeezing out indie producers in ways I have never seen before. They are pretty much making the entire career path economically unviable for the next generation, and that's created a ripple effect in a fragile ecosystem, negatively affecting every other job in the industry. Let's talk more about it. How Hollywood Used to Work We used to have a lot of people taking meetings at Spago, The Ivy, and The Polo Lounge, claiming to be producers with their hands on the hottest spec in town. These were people in expensive suits or cheap suits, but they were suits -- or sometimes flowery dresses. Their hustle allowed them to set up movies at studios in exchange for payment. And eventually, Hollywood thought the best and most sustainable way to do that was to pay them a retainer so they would bring their best ideas to them first. This became known as a first-look deal, and it kept the lights on for producers all over town. We had this even exchange for decades. Independent producers did the heavy lifting in development, and movie studios got to release hits, find new voices, and seem like the smartest in the room. And here's the thing: this worked because money flowed, and people could live in Los Angeles, have families, and take a vacation every year. Producers scouted books, optioned specs, attached talent, refined scripts, and solved production nightmares before a single camera ever rolled. This stuff actually saved studios more than they paid, whether they acknowledged it or no

items.title: A New Kickstarter Campaign is Here to Provide Filmmakers With Their New Mobile Basecamp
items.summary: While this might not be the area of film and video production most direly in need of innovation and change, it never hurts to see new companies come in with fresh ideas and energy. And while familiar names like Pelican with their travel cases and others might still be the top option, if you’re interested in exploring some new ones, then this Crew Gear Box bag series from the Chinese company OPENMOON is quite intriguing. Currently available to support on Kickstarter, let’s look at the OPENMOON Crew Gear Box and explore its goal of becoming a new mobile basecamp for filmmakers. OPENMOON CREW GEAR BOX Bag So, the main calling card of this bag series is that, while it might technically be a “bag,” it’s not your usual soft and floppy bag. The Crew Gear Box is more of a hybrid soft-and-hard case with a rigid structure and locked layout, which should ultimately enable faster set workflows and greater protection and durability. The Kickstarter page is very focused on its “rigid outside, cushioned inside” promise and explains how a layered protection system can provide solid support for your lenses, cameras, and other tools and gear. The other main goal is fast access for fast-moving sets and on-the-run shoots. Along with the structured interior, the bag has some quick-access tool pockets. Also, not for nothing, another neat aspect is that the bag appears to strap easily onto rolling suitcases or utility cases, so traveling with it should be quite manageable. Price and Availability Overall, this is a unique, new offering in the travel bag or case space that looks intriguing at the very least. The Kickstarter page for the product is live now and reports that units should begin shipping here soon, with support prices starting at $229 and going up to $359.

items.title: Is Paramount Skydance Really Preparing to Leave Los Angeles?
items.summary: David Ellison woke up playing hardball, and we're going to learn pretty quickly if he's bluffing or about to change the Hollywood landscape forever. According to a new report by Matt Belloni at Puck (which you really should be following for breaking news), David Ellison has a contingency plan if the $110 billion Paramount–Warner Bros. merger does not go through, and it involves taking his ball and going… anywhere but home. Now, he thinks that the company will ultimately defeat the antitrust lawsuit led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and 11 other Democratic states. But he doesn't want to wait forever for that to close, so he's thinking about going somewhere he won't have to deal with all this stuff. Ellison said that if Bonta refuses to come to the negotiating table by October, Paramount Skydance is prepared to pack up its headquarters and leave California. Let's dive in. The Relocation: Texas, Tennessee, or Georgia? According to Puck, Ellison’s board has already signed off on a strategy to relocate to Tennessee, Texas, Georgia, or another unnamed state offering heavy tax incentives. It would take five years, but his goal was to take most of the 30,000 jobs with him. The start would be corporate HQ, and the rest would trickle from there. Now, this seems crazy. You are a Hollywood studio. What the hell are you going to do in one of these other places that's not Hollywood? But if it means they can close their deal or save hundreds of millions of dollars, they don't care. They can Zoom like the rest of the town, and I am sure they'll just fly execs in and out of the office if they have to see someone in person. In fact, he has a blueprint to do this, because it's what his Dad did with Oracle. They left CA but kept a creative hub here, and Paramount would do the same. items.title: YouTube Announces Changes to Partner Program, Including Raising Requirements for Earning Revenue
items.summary: In many ways, YouTube is pretty much the big-all, end-all of content creation these days. It’s so ingrained in our everyday lives we probably take it for granted more than we think, yet at every turn—there it is. For current or aspiring content creators, it's of endless importance and, to the company’s credit (or Google’s credit), it’s still one of the top destinations for content creators to go to if they’d like to actually get a relatively fair split of the ad revenue their content brings in. And while that split isn’t changing just yet (although YouTube could certainly change that at a moment's notice), the requirements for new creators to be a part of this revenue-earning Partner Program are about to change. Here’s what you need to know. YouTube Partner Program Changes Starting on February 1st, 2027, YouTube announced that creators will need 8,000 watch hours over 12 months or 20 million Short views in 90 days to be eligible for the Partner Program and its revenue-sharing. There are also some other changes coming which YouTube has outlined with these distinctions for what’s going to be different, and what’s going to remain the same: What’s changing: More opportunity for subscription revenue through premium lite Rolling minimum performance requirement to earn monthly on Shorts Entry thresholds for new YPP channels for ads and premium revenue What’s not changing: Revenue share split across long-form and Shorts Eligibility for fan funding and shopping products Channel’s existing YPP status The other changes concern YouTube Premium Lite and Shorts. YouTube Premium Lite and Shorts First, let’s look at Premium Lite, which YouTube is rolling out to all countries where YouTube Premium is currently offered and will offer uninterrupted, offline, and background viewing of most content. items.title: Sennheiser Announces That It Is Now the Official Sound Provider of Formula E
items.summary: In exciting news for anyone who follows pro racing, or in this case specifically pro electric racing, Sennheiser, the global audio specialty company best known to filmmakers and content creators for its microphones and audio solutions, has announced that it is signing a multi-year partnership with Formula E. If you aren't super familiar, Formula E is the highest-class open-wheel single-seater motorsport championship for electric cars and a growing brand in the pro racing world. Let’s look at what this partnership entails and what it could bring for the future of both brands. Sennheiser Partners With Formula E Launched back in 2014, Formula E is indeed a fast-growing and very entertaining part of the world of professional racing these days. This collaboration between the brands will see the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship integrate Sennheiser’s professional audio solutions and next-gen AMBEO immersive audio technology across the global series with the goal of creating new ways for fans to experience the excitement, energy and emotion of electric racing. “Formula E represents exactly the kind of environment where meaningful innovation happens. At Sennheiser, we are driven by the ambition to bring advanced audio technologies into real-world applications, and this collaboration gives us an exciting opportunity to rethink the role sound can play in electric racing. Great visuals deserve equally compelling sound, and we see real potential to define the sport’s unique acoustic character through dynamic in-car and trackside soundscapes. Ultimately, this partnership is about learning, exploring and helping to shape the future of how live sport is experienced.” - Andreas Sennheiser, CEO of the Sennheiser Group. The goal of the partnership seems to be not just to provide audio solutions, but to enable both brands to explore how advanced audio capture and encoding workflows can create more immersive experiences for viewers on any device. items.title: Why ‘Reacher’ is Already an Action Masterpiece That Matches the Ethos of '80s and '90s Classics
items.summary: The fourth season of Amazon Prime’s Reacher is set to come out this week, and it’s got us thinking about how Alan Ritchson’s larger-than-life portrayal of the titular character from Lee Child’s pulp novel series isn’t just homaging the action classics of the 80s and 90s; it’s in many ways taking the reins and charting a path for something new. While we admittedly all have soft spots in our hearts for the iconic action films of Arnold Schwarzenegger, Sylvester Stallone, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and others from the “ultimate era” of the '80s and '90s, it’s obvious that era is long gone at this point. And despite a few promising entries over the years with the likes of Jason Bourne and John Wick, we really haven’t seen a new action hero emerge worthy of this pedigree. That is, until Reacher showed up. The Growing Legacy of Jack Reacher Based on the titular character in the Jack Reacher novel series, first published in 1997 by Lee Child, Reacher has always been a larger-than-life character deserving of a portrayal on the biggest of screens. And that’s exactly what the character got with Tom Cruise taking on the role in the Christopher McQuarrie-written and directed first action thriller of a two-film series. However, while the films—I’d argue—do quite well enough in their own rights, they’re lacking one element which was always going to be the case. Tom Cruise isn’t big. Reacher is big. Alan Ritchson, like the action stars like Arnie and Stallone who came before him, is big. And, for better or for worse, that’s a huge element of what makes the character so notable, so iconic, and ultimately just work. 'Reacher' Season 4 Debuting on August 12th, 2026, Reacher Season 4 is based on Gone Tomorrow, the thirteenth novel in the Jack Reacher Series by Child, and is set to follow Reacher try to solve yet another death mystery, this time in New York. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The 'Good, the Bad and the Ugly' Line That Proved Fate Can Change in an Instant
items.summary: Sometimes the simplest lines in a movie can hit the hardest, and today's example is one such line. It's from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and is spoken by the man with probably the least use for it. Near the beginning of the movie, as a crowd gathers to watch an outlaw hang, a woman on a passing stagecoach says she's glad they finally caught him. The bounty killer beside her hardly reacts. "People with ropes around their necks don't always hang," he says. It's tossed off, delivered with total calm, and might not feel important in the moment. But in Sergio Leone's West, a noose is never the last word. Let's look closer. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Scene Early in the film, the coolheaded Blondie (Clint Eastwood) runs a dangerous routine with Tuco (Eli Wallach), the loudmouth bandit he's partnered with for profit. In at least 15 different counties, the scam goes like this. Blondie hands Tuco over to the law, collects the reward on his wanted head, and waits for the hanging. Then, as the trapdoor is about to drop, Blondie picks off the rope with a single rifle shot from a rooftop, and the two of them ride off to run it again in the next town. The line arrives during the second time we see this scam running. A public official reads out Tuco's long list of crimes (and y'all, it's bad if you haven't seen the movie in a while). Tuco is sentenced to hang by the neck until dead. A woman on a stagecoach, watching, says she's glad they captured such a terrible man. "Glad they got him. A man guilty of all those crimes!" Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef's ice-cold bounty hunter) is climbing aboard the same coach, and he already sees the whole con. He says, "People with ropes around their necks don't always hang." "What do you mean?" she asks. "Even a filthy beggar like that has a protecting angel," he says. His eyes find Blondie in position across the square. "A golden-haired angel watches over him." And before Tuco hangs, Blondie rescues him again. What the Line Reveals About Angel
